utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, I see that you're alone. Mr. Piletta-Zanin will arrive, or is he -- you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Piletta-Zanin will arrive. He did not realise that there was a change in schedule. My colleague had his ticket for the morning because the earlier schedule said that we would be working in the afternoon. So that is why he is not here. But I'm sure he will arrive by the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our monitors are not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true for mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But some of the Judges do have monitors that are --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technician is working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it's functioning, Ms. Pilipovic. Then I think the -- if the Prosecution is ready to continue the cross-examination of Witness DP6, then please, Mr. Usher, escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. DP6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. And the counsel for the Prosecution will now continue your cross-examination. Mr. Ierace, please proceed. And statement, I see that the screens -- our screens are partially gone again. I take it that the technicians will take care that we -- well, at least we have still got -- let's move on even if it's not -- if the screen is not working -- yes, it is now. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the last occasion you told us that the school for blind children or the home for blind children was outside your part of the front line. Why, then, did you go there so often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I was there all that often. I would go there once a week to see to things and talk about things. And besides, I had friends there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that you had friends there, why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to see their positions too and where the fire was coming -- or going from and so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said last week that on the first floor you couldn't set guards there because of security. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say about this -- because the hospital and buildings across the street from us, they dominated over us. And if you're on the first floor, you see further than if you're on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why was there a need for security if you wanted to go upstairs in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of the gunfire, because -- because they could see us better if we were on the first floor than if we were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in the closest of the buildings to your part of the front line, there were two floors above the ground floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And there were members of the SRK firing from those floors, were there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those two top floors?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that we were downstairs on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we only opened fire when fire was opened against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's not my question. I'm putting to you that there were members of the SRK firing from the upper two floors.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Prosecutor, I was in those -- in Nedzarici and I know where the fire came from, at least when I was on my front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with the claim because from the upper floors we dared not fire, fearing for our own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Last week, you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because one observed from the upper floors, one goes up, looks around, and takes shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Upstairs there were internal walls as well as the exterior walls, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, interior? There was exterior and then there was partitions inside between classrooms. If you mean the institute for the blind, there were classrooms and dormitories for the children. There was one exterior wall and there were partitions inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that there were shooters in the internal rooms positioned so that there were two walls between them and the outside as you faced east towards the ABiH front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two walls? Not one building had two walls. One -- they had only one wall, the chief wall, that is, the exterior walls which were either brick walls or concrete. And then -- in front there was the facade and there was nothing. What two walls? There were no two walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you were very familiar with the layout of the institute for blind children before the war, weren't you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that last reply has to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, would you please take care of that, lines -- page 4, line 25 up till 5, second line. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that in the building closest to your part of the front line there were shooters in the internal rooms firing through openings in the internal walls and then through windows on the external wall towards the ABiH front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the beginning of your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. In the building of the institute for blind children, closest to your part of the front line, there were SRK shooters operating from the internal rooms upstairs, firing through openings made in those internal walls, and then through windows on the external wall towards the ABiH front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fired when we had to. Those people fired when they had to fire at the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So let me put it to you this way: You cannot deny that from time to time there was firing from that building, can you, because you weren't there all the time, for a start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I wasn't. But we were close enough. And when there was shooting, one could recognise where the fire came from, because I was pretty familiar with Nedzarici. I'd lived there for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you it is absurd to say that the SRK fired from the ground floor but did not fire from the upper two storeys. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also and likewise claim that the fire was opened from the ground floor and that the upper floors mostly were used to observe. And I've just explained why we couldn't fire from upper floors, because there were tall buildings dominating and one could see everything through the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So the very reasons that made the upper storeys ideal for observation made them also ideal for firing at ABiH positions, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? What did you say, this last thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The height afforded by the upper two storeys made it an ideal position for both observation and for shooting at ABiH positions, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that they were ideal, but we could not fire from those upper floors because of what I just said, because of those tall buildings. We could not stay there long enough to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As it is, you have told us that the institute buildings attracted fire on a daily basis. Why would they fire at that building if there were not positions occupied by the SRK for shooting at ABiH positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was opened on the positions of the BH Army when they opened fire first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you have to ask them why they did it. And we had to defend ourselves, so we had to open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you have no explanation as to why they fired on that building on a daily basis, given your evidence that there was not shooting from the two upper storeys; is that correct? Not that you saw, in any event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Fire was not opened from the upper two floors. I said that shooting was done from the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, last week you told us that you received orders from your battalion commander, I think it was, to not hit civilians. Were those orders received in writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was usually done by induction telephone, that is, when one calls from telephone to say not to open fire against civilians, women and children, because that was strictly prohibited to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it ever done in writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, truth to tell, I don't remember it was done in writing, but I guess the battalion command received it from the brigade command and they then would call us by inductor, because those inductor telephones were connected serially.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you regard it as a standing order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a standing order. Such orders were issued -- well, every day. Well, not every day exactly, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have told us how immediately opposite your part of the front line there were high-rise buildings on the ABiH side. Before the war, were they residential apartment buildings, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And during the war, civilians continued to live in that same area, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first buildings, the buildings which were on the front lines, those buildings had been moved out, that is, people left because there was gunfire. They went to the countryside.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Between September 1992 and February --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these buildings -- sorry. In those front buildings, the troops were there in those buildings. I mean, Muslim troops were in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Between September 1992 and February 1993, did you ever see a person on the ABiH side whom you believed to be a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was it that you said? Between September and ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: September 1992 and February 1993, from your position on your part of the front line, did you ever see civilians on the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used to see them but not all that much, because it was -- I mean, there were screens and containers obstructing. People did that so that they could move about safely, and one didn't really see them much, both civilians -- equally civilians and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Up until February 1993, when you saw ABiH military, were they wearing uniforms or not wearing uniforms, or a combination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by and large they wore uniforms. I mean, if they were military, they wore uniforms, uniforms and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Between September 1992 and February 1993, did you ever fire on a person not in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't. We didn't, because we had strict orders not to fire at civilians, women, and children. They kept telling us over the telephone that we were not to fire on civilians, women, and children, and we didn't as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, if you saw a male of military age not wearing a uniform, you did not fire upon that person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't, because you cannot see whether a man is of military age or not, because if you see someone at a distance, you can see that it's a civilian, then naturally you don't fire at him because that is what our orders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you accept that if there was any doubt in your mind as to whether the person you could see was military or civilian, if there was any doubt, then you should not target that person; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, one was not supposed to open fire then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Madam Pilipovic last week whether there was any investigation in that period, September 1992 to February 1993, any investigation as to the possible shooting of civilians, and you replied that your orders were to not shoot civilians. Could you please answer the question directly: Are you aware of any investigation carried out within the SRK as to the possible shooting of any civilians on the ABiH side by SRK forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear stories of any investigations of that nature in that time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying to follow the examination by my learned friend as far as I can remember. There were no questions about investigations to this witness. So with my apologies, I'd like my learned friend to say on which side and when was that. Or perhaps during a break we could find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you ask the witness to take his headphones off for a second, and you'd like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if I have the page. It's page 53 in my hard copy from the 16th of - excuse me - from the 16th of October, but those pages don't match. Mr. Mundis will locate it. I'll read the question. That might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Mr. DP6, when your subordinates reported to you about the situation in their areas of responsibility, did you ever get a report that somebody had hit a civilian or that some civilians -- that there were some civilian casualties? Did you ever receive such a report?" Answer: "Excuse me. I said a moment ago that we were forbidden to fire at civilians, the elderly and children. I said that a moment ago."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection by Ms. Pilipovic is that there was nothing about investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's true, Mr. President. There wasn't mention of the word "investigation." Rather, a reference to reports of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that if nothing is reported, that there would be no need to investigate? Or is that -- I still have some difficulties with the link between negative answer on your question or reporting and investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the need for an investigation may arise without reports from within the SRK. The need for investigation can arise by, for instance, notice worthy of investigation coming from UNPROFOR. But I must say that I think it was inappropriate for me to use the word "investigation" in the sense that my learned colleague had included that in a question. And for that, I apologise. It's more a question of reports. But Mr. President, I would persevere with my last question, which is not contingent upon that answer, that last question being essentially, did he ever hear of any investigations within the SRK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that then touch upon the subject matter covered in chief, or would this be a 90(H) case of the Prosecution question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the -- if you're asking me what the relevance of the question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. The relevance is this: That there is some -- first of all, the accused in the pre-trial brief filed by the Defence has said that there was no need for any investigation of allegations of targeting of civilians by his subordinates because no one ever gave him sufficient information to allow such an investigation to take place. However, we have heard in the Prosecution case a large body of evidence of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. notice in what I anticipate the Trial Chamber would accept was sufficient detail of such incidents to warrant an investigation; in other words, that a reasonable commander in the position of the accused at the time of receiving that notice would have felt obliged to take what steps were in his power to carry out an investigation. Given that evidence, it is appropriate to enquire whether in fact any investigations were carried out. Secondly, there is some evidence in the Prosecution case that the accused indeed acknowledged that there was a need for investigation and said that he would investigate, although no response or no follow-up was ever made available to the complainers. So that's the -- the relevance of it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, but let's just keep in mind that on the last issue on the upper floors, it took a lot of time, where it -- I wondered at a certain moment whether it would assist any further to put any further questions to the witness in that respect. Would you please keep that in mind if you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. And the page reference is 13903 at line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. I notice Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence's question is if my learned colleague can tell me which witnesses of the Prosecution stated that they reported to any body responsible for reporting incidents. The Defence questions to all the Prosecution witnesses were, even if there was some kind of incident that took place: Did they ever inform anybody that this incident had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the questions asked by the Defence of victims and witnesses were to the effect as to whether they reported it to the UN or to the police. The notice to which I refer is notice given to General Galic personally or to his senior subordinates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just try to shortcut. Do I understand you, Mr. Ierace, that you're referring to the evidence which is reports not always of specific incidents but of -- attacks on civilians by sniping, is the word that was used by witnesses, or was in the question rather than specific incidents being reported? And while Ms. Pilipovic is asking -- is referring to specific incidents, rather than to general complaints at the higher levels in the SRK about sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In a general sense, that's so. There is some more specific information according to the evidence that was passed on to the senior echelons of SRK, including the accused. But essentially, it is as you've put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed and keep in mind what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you told us that when you could not see the source of fire from the -- I'll start again. I think you just put your headphones on. You told us that when you could not see the source of fire from the ABiH side, on those occasions sometimes it was possible to hear where the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How would you respond in those circumstances? In other words, would you return fire to a source that you could not see but you judged according to the sound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually we would wait and try to hear where the fire was coming from. And then if it was necessary for us to open fire, we would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it that -- I'm sorry. I take it that -- well, when you say you would open fire, do you mean with small arms or with mortars or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Including mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars would be used only when this was necessary. They would not be used in the case of these, I don't know, small, minor provocations. As long as we could defend ourselves with infantry weapons, then we would only use those weapons. Because we had to justify that. You couldn't just shoot anyhow. You would always have to justify the ammunition used, how much of it was spent, why, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to that in a moment. When you arranged or ordered for mortar fire to be used, in particular where you could not see the source of fire but could only hear it, what steps, if any, did you take to assess whether mortar fire would pose risks or could pose risks to civilians in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't order for the mortars to be used. The command of the battalion would be informed first and then the battalion command would decide. But if it was necessary to use mortar fire, once we assessed where the firing was coming from - because there were maps - then we would say where the firing was coming from. These were more or less positions of the B and H Army. So we would fire at those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The maps presumably were reasonably detailed in terms of the territory of the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say, I personally knew where their positions were. Those were the buildings in front of us and where the firing was coming from. And as I said, I would inform the battalion the firing is coming from -- usually we would mark those buildings with numbers 1, 2, 3, or A, B, C, so we would say that the firing was coming from such and such a building. And then I don't know how the procedure then continued as far as the mortars were concerned, but that's -- that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The fire that hit those buildings in front of you after September 1992, you've told us, set them alight, the gunfire. What particular types of weapons caused the buildings to catch alight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buildings were set on fire both by the infantry weapons and by the mortars, not just by the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Apart from mortars -- please wait. Apart from mortar, was artillery used against those high-rise buildings in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What artillery weapons? What are you -- what do you -- what are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Weapons such as Howitzers or tanks or field guns.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The anti-aircraft guns were not used. They -- we didn't even have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The student hostels you have told us contained ABiH positions. Were not -- was not artillery used against those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I really don't know. I don't think that they were used, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, a mortar is not a particularly effective weapon against a high-rise building, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the buildings, that is, the high-rise buildings opposite your position and further along Ante Babica Street, were targeted with direct fire artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that for as long as I was there, that was not the case, because it is impossible. I don't know -- I don't know -- with a tank or something else to fire at the student hostel. I don't know where you would be able to fire from for a tank to come close in order to fire at the student hostel, since this settlement was in Nedzarici and there were no tanks at Nedzarici, so the grenade couldn't go between the houses in order to hit the student hostel or a high-rise building, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence to only cover the period up until February of 1993, that is, that aspect of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the period between September and February 28th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And then in your answer -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript doesn't seem to record a reference by the witness to 1993. Perhaps it will come out in the corrected transcript. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see in page 16, line 24 that the witness said: "You asked me about the period between September and February 28th, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. In the previous long answer there was a reference to 1993. In any event ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the student building -- of the two student buildings, at least the southernmost, did not have walls, only floors, by late 1993. In other words, it was possible to see through the building across the internal floors from one side to the other. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could you see through the building? This is really not clear to me. You could not see through the building. For me to be able to see from here - and there's a wall there - for me to be able to see somewhere is there 500 or 1.000 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You understand that it's a high-rise building, that is, the -- both buildings are of a similar construction, with concrete floors and walls between those floors, so that the building could continue to stand if the walls were removed. And I suggest to you that's what happened; the building was constantly attacked, to a point where it was possible to look through the building, across the floors.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that it was not possible to see. I said the last time that that building also was on fire, the walls were black, and also on top of that you couldn't see. How could you possibly see through it? There's no way that you can. The building across from me also was a student hostel, so it was the same. It was made of cement blocks. So it wasn't possible to see through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you -- I withdraw that. Whilst you were on that part of the front line, did you ever see vehicles on the other side of the confrontation line which did not have any military markings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not see the vehicles because this was -- I am repeating this for I don't know how many times. Barriers were erected, paravents, containers, so that it wasn't possible to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Barriers were not 100 per cent effective in terms of blocking your view though, were they? There were gaps in the barriers, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see the -- in the places where one came next to the other. But there were gaps between the boards or the cars or whatever. But they were not very big. It wasn't possible to see much. I know what we did. If there are joints, then you would place blankets or something at those places in order to make the gap where things could be visible only 2 or 3 centimetres wide or perhaps 5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There was nothing in the standing orders that you received in relation to civilians that prevented you from targeting military vehicles on the ABiH side, was there, if you had seen them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were orders, like I said before, not to fire at civilians. Military vehicles -- nobody said, "fire at military vehicles". But if they opened fire at us, we had to fire back. We had to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you had seen a truck with civilian markings on it, such as a delivery van, in terms of the orders that you received, would there be anything preventing you from hitting such a vehicle, a civilian vehicle with markings suggesting a delivery truck?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend asked about written orders, but Witness DP6 said that there were never any written orders that they received but that they mostly received orders over the telephone. So I think that this matter might be creating some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In my transcript and in my understanding of the English language used, it was just about orders and not about written orders. Is that correct, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you have regarded a civilian -- I withdraw that. Would you have regarded a -- what appeared to be a delivery truck of a civilian nature as being a target prohibited by the orders you received had you seen such a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was civilian, naturally we would not fire at; anything that was civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I take it in determining whether or not something was civilian, you were guided by the appearance, whether it's a person or whether it's a vehicle carrying persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In determining -- I'll confine it to a vehicle. In determining whether a vehicle travelling along a road is an appropriate target, you'd be guided by the appearance of that vehicle, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You told us last week that you had to report your expenditure of ammunition. Did you do that in writing or did you do that just by voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would notify by telephone the brigade command. We would say on such and such a day so much 7.62 or 7.9 ammunition was spent and they would write that down at the brigade command, how much was spent and what for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So you did it by phone to the brigade command and you understood that the brigade did it in writing, in terms of going further up the chain from there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question that the Defence wishes to ask; of course, with your permission. We would like to use the presence of this witness and see if he can tell us how far the theological faculty was away from the front line held by the company, the company of Witness DP6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, we have a lot of maps. Is there disagreement between the parties as to the distance between these two buildings on the map? Because otherwise it will give no more precise information. So I wonder whether this is something where we are much assisted by the perhaps precise, perhaps unprecise, knowledge of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure that we've marked on the map the theological institute. I have no objection to the witness doing that, if he could, if it's not already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. Ms. Pilipovic, you could perhaps ask the witness to mark it on the map and then I'd say we'll measure what the distance approximately is. I think that's preferable than to know that it's 300 or 700 or -- well, whatever distance. Please proceed then. Could perhaps the witness be shown that same map. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is D1760, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If we could perhaps identify the relevant marking which is already on the map, Mr. President, in terms of the printed map. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I do not see the -- well, if the parties would agree -- now, let me just ask the witness to take off his headphones. If the parties would agree that a building which answers "fakultet" on the map, which that would be the building, then it's -- there's no need at all. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's ask the witness if that building, where it states "teoloski fakultet," "the theological faculty."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have any more questions than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DP6, this place where "fakultet" ends --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Could you place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP6, could you please tell us, this place where the word "fakultet" ends, is that the theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've now lost the picture. For the sake of the record, the witness was pointing with his finger to a place on the map where it reads "Teoloski Fakultet."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP6, could you please tell us, how far is the theological faculty away from the line, the front line where you say your company was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 800 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to Olimpijska Street, the place where the word "Mojmilo" is. That's where the Olimpijska Street is. So in relation to that street, the beginning of that street, how far is the theological faculty from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 1400 or 1500 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps the witness might remove his earphones quickly, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, could you take off your earphones for a second. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a map that's been provided by the Defence. I would be grateful if the Defence could say that they accept that each of the squares indicated on the map is 1 kilometre by 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment I don't have the whole map in front of me in order to check whether the squares are 1 by 1 kilometre. I could do that in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is only half the map. And once I check that, then in future that will not be something that is disputed, that each square represents 1 kilometre. But at this point, I am not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you what further information you would have if you have got the whole map? I mean, what would that change, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we have the scale on the map somewhere, when we have the map as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. If you want to have the scale. Just perhaps for your guidance on other maps, I usually took the runway of the airport as being approximately 2 and a half kilometres and that is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I ask that is if it's common ground that whatever the scale indicated is the scale, then I don't seek leave to ask any more questions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you'll be able to agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to say that we don't have the squares here. They are not the squares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I understood to be the squares, the blue lines. But if that is not what you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I take your point. They're not quite square. And therefore, I'll be guided by the scale of the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not entirely. I do agree. They're almost squares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, the Judges also have some questions for you. Judge Nieto-Navia will first put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you have the map? No, you don't. The map, yes. And I think that we need a thin pen, green or red or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Green would be a perfect colour, perhaps, for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, you'll told us that there were some barriers, screens, and containers and things like that at the Ante Babica Street. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Would you draw a line showing that barrier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every intersection from which I could -- one could see streets coming together, these barriers were put up, as we called them, containers or screens. And here too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I'd like you to tell me about some details. You said that you and your comrades were equipped with weapons, with rifles. Who was it, you or your comrades? How did you organise yourselves? Spontaneously, or did you depend on a group which was linked with the headquarters, with the staff? Could you tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were organised in the Territorial Defence, and I and my comrades -- I and my colleagues -- I'm talking about those men with whom I was together on Lukavicka Cesta as the Territorial Defence. And later on when the army, when the Yugoslav People's Army, pulled out of the barracks, we were told that we should go to fetch the weapons. And we went to the barracks and we went in groups, not all at once. We were in groups of 10 or 15. So we go there, get the weapons, then the next group goes there and takes weapons for it and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you well, you always depended on the Romanija Corps, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So the orders came to you from the corps staff via the brigade, battalion, down to the company; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know where the orders came from. All I know is that we were told to go to the barracks to get those weapons. I really do not know where the orders came, whether it was the corps command or something else. I mean, it was a higher instance. I was just an ordinary soldier and I was also told to go there. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You were shown a photograph too. On this photograph, there were one or two houses which were destroyed in part, and you told us that you recognised them, that it was in a part of Nedzarici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember -- that is, did you tell us that those buildings and that destruction happened in Nedzarici, or did you yourself recognise the place, the buildings specifically shown in that particular photograph? I do not know if I am quite clear. Perhaps I will rephrase my question? Do you want me to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember a photograph showing buildings partially destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the -- D1762 will be shown to the witness. Perhaps it could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So yes, it is this photograph here. Do you recognise the exact place, or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph, can you confirm to us, can you really say that this photograph represents a neighbourhood or buildings that you recognise in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: And do you think that these buildings were on the front line? Were they in the protected area, or were those buildings where the front line was, buildings that you used as trenches against buildings across the street or across -- against the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These buildings were right next to the front line, these houses here, right next to it. They followed Lukavicka -- they were on Lukavicka Cesta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were behind your lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They were right on the front line, right next to the front line, because all the front houses, all the front houses burnt down by summer, by September. All the houses that were in front had been put fire to and burnt down, those which were along the front line. And in the rear you would find a house burnt down here and there. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you took shelter in those buildings there, didn't you? So these are buildings which one could say were part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now a question: To your knowledge, do you see if there were any women who participated in the fighting on the other side, I mean, on the -- on the side of the army of the presidency? Were there any women participating in the -- in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side? On the BH Army side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, on the BH Army side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't know -- how could I? I didn't know whether they participated or not. I really couldn't. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you yourself, you did not see any women combatants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, I've got a few questions for you as well. Could perhaps be put on the ELMO again the map, D1760. Mr. DP6, you told us about barriers that were erected on your side. Could you tell us where these barriers were and how they were erected, by these containers or cars or whatever. But first, where were they put? Could you point at it with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates] These barriers of ours were put where I was, here. Here, along this street, then here also, along this street, then lengthwise. Since we could not walk the street -- walk around the streets in Nedzarici, we put the screens or barriers, as you call them, between houses, so that we would zigzag between the houses and around the houses to get to, say, the rear of Nedzarici or the command or get to Ilidza to have a bath, if there happened to be water and so on and so forth. And in these streets that I showed here, they were put up here and here. In Nedzarici there weren't all that many long streets. Between houses in Nedzarici, we also put them up there where we wanted to pass by so that the other side couldn't see us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they effective?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, more or less. But we usually moved around at night. We took shifts -- we changed shifts at night and we moved around at night, because all around we had all those high-rise buildings, no matter how high were our screens, one could see us from above, because the beginning of the war taught us that. We had very low barriers, then we realised they served no purpose. And besides, there was also wind and they would fall down and so -- so that we mostly moved around at night. We changed guards at night. At night we delivered food, so that -- because that was when we could move about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how were they made? You said wind, and that suggests that sheets were used. Did you also use containers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, yes. In the rear, we used mostly sheets, or blankets. And on the high street, on the main street, we used containers and blankets and some other screens. But inside Nedzarici it was usually some blankets or some plywood or some other boards, so that the wind wouldn't turn them upside down and then we would keep them -- hold them together with wire or some rope or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be -- first of all, for the sake of the record, when the witness pointed at places where barriers were erected, he was pointing at side roads where they issue on the Lukavicka Cesta, on where he indicated sometimes before. Those coming from a south-westerly direction. My next question would be: You have told repeatedly that there was a strict prohibition to fire at civilians and those who had a civilian appearance. This Chamber has heard some evidence of people with a civilian appearance being hit quite close to where these confrontation lines were. Would you have an explanation as how they were hit where you were under strict prohibition to fire at whatever person with a civilian appearance or object with a civilian appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, but - and I'm being very truthful - there were such orders, and we heeded them, and I always emphasise it. And when we had meetings, I mean company commanders with the battalion commander, he always pointed that out. He always emphasised that we were not to fire on civilians, at women, at children, at the elderly, that this was not done. But now I can't say whether individuals did fire at them, because I really didn't know that. I didn't know that. Or did somebody tell me that he'd hit a civilian or a woman or a child? Nobody ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that -- perhaps not on an everyday basis but quite frequently these orders were repeated. Would you have an explanation why it had to be repeated so frequently if this order was always strictly obeyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably -- as likely as not. I don't really know. I only know that it was repeated frequently. I suppose somebody suggested it to somebody, that somebody suggested it to the battalion command, and that is why they did it all that often. But I really don't know why was it so often and how was it that it was so often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. DP6. This concludes your examination in this court. I know that that was a very long examination for you. You spent here altogether, well, not a full four days but at least two full days and two parts of a day. I thank you very much for coming and for answering all the questions, both of the parties and the Judges, since it is important for this Court to hear the testimony of those who have been present at the relevant times and at the relevant places. So thank you very much, and I hope you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to thank you for treating me decently, and I'd like to thank all those present. And I'd most of all like to thank those girls who meet us, who welcome us in that little room, who help us relax, talk with us. But otherwise, everything was fine. Everything was great. So thank you very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll tell the unit that you're very happy with the way they treated you. Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. All the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's any other issue to be discussed at this very moment, we'll adjourn until 11.00. And I then take it that the Defence is ready to call its next witness. And that will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is in fact an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whether measures should be granted. Perhaps we should go into private session now or when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll do that when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before doing so, there was one outstanding issue of some information still to be provided by the Defence to the Prosecution, if I remember well. There's the map, but there was another issue, I think, in respect of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And that hasn't been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It hasn't been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And that's relevant to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd first -- then for the remaining two minutes, I'd like to turn into private or closed session, which is the same in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. My issue would be that we still have to decide on the exhibits presented to Witness DP6. Mr. Ierace, what would you like to raise in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm informed by the Defence that the appropriate scale for the map that was used with the last witness is 1 to 20.000, and I'm grateful for that. And this afternoon I anticipate that the Prosecution will file some -- some information in relation to protective measures, issues which may assist the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. We have to deal with the exhibits from Witness DP6. Madam Registrar, could you please indicate to us which witness -- which documents were tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right. One is P3752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And then D1759. That is the pseudonym name sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And then D1760. It's a map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We just talked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is 1762 the right number? I've got one copy which says 1760, but -- do find out about the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1760 is the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We used a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is a photo of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't it true that 1760 was tendered in relation to this witness as well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, marked by him. Okay. If there are no objections, all these documents are admitted into evidence. Then Mr. Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, am I correct, all these exhibits need to be entered under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have to be -- I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't think the map is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map is certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the Defence agree? Yes. Then that's not under seal. Is the marking of -- the photographs are not under seal either, are they? It's only the name sheet, I think, that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that one is under seal and the other exhibits are admitted without any restriction.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So only D1759 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And then P3752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply, I wish to remind you of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is, with regard to Exhibit 1762, the Defence has indicated that they did not intend to tender it as an exhibit. I don't know if we are talking about the second photograph. It's simply a formal matter. If the Prosecution wishes to tender it so that we -- but I think it's important to make it known that we are not the ones who are tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm happy to tender that photograph as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, one question has been put to the witness by the Bench as well, so therefore it might be wise to have it admitted into evidence. So if you tender -- then we'll have to change the number again in the P number. Would the Defence be willing, although it's not vital for their case, to tender that document into evidence? Otherwise we'll change the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We accept it. We shall be happy to accept that. It was merely to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then it's admitted as D1762. I apologise for you, Mr. Witness. I'll not use your name. First of all, may I ask you whether you can hear me a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to use your name, since protective measures have been granted in respect of you. That means that no one out of this courtroom can see your face and that we'll not mention your name. Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The usher will now hand out the text of this declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since the protective measures have been granted to you, the Defence wishes to show you a document to look at your particulars on it and confirm that they are correct, and we shall, both we and the Prosecution, will address you as DP4, rather than by your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes. These are my particulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence merely wishes to say that when I finish, my colleague will also ask a few questions, with your leave, as before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence would like to go into private session for Mr. DP4 to tell us something about himself, where he lives, where he was born, where he worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn in to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, you told us that until the -- that before the war you worked -- you told us where you worked. Can you tell us briefly when, according to you, the conflict broke out in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, the real conflict started towards the end of April or in the early days of May. But from the beginning of April, we started feeling the tension mount, but the proper conflict started in the early days of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the real conflict started in the early days of May," can you tell us specifically in the part of the city that you lived in, did something happen there, in the beginning of May, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Concretely, on the 14th of May, Muslim forces tried to take our neighbourhood on a large scale, presumably to get to the Sarajevo airport because of its strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the 14th of May," that there was an attack on your locality, can you tell us what you did, that is, you personally, what did you undertake? And if you know, what did other citizens in the area do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The inhabitants in our neighbourhood community organised themselves in the beginning. That is, throughout April there was some kind of guards mounted. We had good relations with Stupska Petlja neighbourhood community, which was predominantly Muslim and Croat, but we nevertheless mounted guards to be on the safe side. We were not particularly well armed. Until the 14th of May, there were no open attacks and we didn't expect any. But on the 14th of May, their forces came early, accompanied by an APC. They were well armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you tell us what kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, I had an ordinary rifle, M-48, which we were issued by the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you had a rifle M-48 that you were issued with by the civil defence, can you tell us when were you issued with it and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I was issued with the rifle in the neighbourhood communities premises in Nedzarici in mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your other neighbours, if I may call them that. Do you know how they got armed -- or rather, were they armed and how did they come by their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: They were armed in part. Members of the reserve police across Sarajevo had automatic rifles which they took home, that is, those policemen had automatic rifles. Individuals had [inaudible] or perhaps hunting weapons and some pistols and also some of the weapons of the civil defence, which the neighbourhood community staff somehow procured. I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, you told us that Nedzarici was attacked on the 14th of May and that Muslims had [inaudible] arms. Can you tell us from which positions did you reject an attack, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but I'd like to say that we are not getting anything from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a specific problem? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I reply to the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. DP4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Specifically, the attack was repulsed in the area of [inaudible] and the flower shop, behind the family houses where we lived, this specific attack on my line, that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, I wanted to ask you certain questions about your line. You say that you were self-organised. How many of you were there on that line of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: There were about 30 of us on my line, on this specific position, which we later formed after this attack and we stayed there until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, when you said that you formed your line and that it stayed there in that place until the end of the war, can you please tell us whether there were any and what were the positions of the other side. How shall I put it? When you were talking about defence now and the attacks which were directed against you. Can you please a little more specific and clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Specifically, in the area where I was throughout the war, their lines were the newly built cement facilities of Cenex then the market, the house of Ikic across the street from the market, and then new facilities, the Betonara, the cement works and other facilities such as the fire tower. They even fired at us from the -- the refrigerating plant at Stup.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, when you say that there were 30 of you at your line, can you please tell us how you were organised. Were you organised into a formation and what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In that period, we were not organised as a real military formation. People simply, in that part of the neighbourhood where they lived, formed a kind of guard, a defence guard in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you became a real formation. When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: There was some kind of structuring into a proper army during the month of June 1992, although only at the end of September 1992 could an increased level of military organisation be sensed. Discipline, certain requested for us or demands upon us as soldiers, our responsibility and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said "towards us as soldiers," can you tell us how you were dressed as soldiers. Did you have any characteristic indications or markings that you were soldiers, insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the beginning we were not dressed as proper soldiers. If somebody did have that, they had that from being a part of the reserve forces and that's what they were able to wear. So it was all mixed. Some people were in civilian clothes, some people had some kind of military or police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the name of the formation that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In our neighbourhood our battalion, our unit was called Battalion Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "battalion," were you organised at your line as a battalion or a part of a battalion, or did you have a formation which had a certain title and belonged to the battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: We were organised into companies and we communicated through them and received information back from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which company did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: To the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, if I showed you a map of Sarajevo, would you be able to indicate and mark to us on that map the place or the line where you were, as well as the places from where there were actions by the members of the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I show you a map, the Defence would like to point out that we are talking about the period in 1992, September 1993 and 1994. And if you can tell us whether in that period the front lines on one or the other side moved. And this is according to what you know because these lines -- you were there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be a translation issue, but the way the English was translated and indeed transcribed, it reads "the period in 1992, September 1993 and 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a mistake. It was September 1992, 1993, 1994. I can see it in the transcript. I think that was the way I put my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, the Defence would like to show you a map. Could you please mark on this map the line, the front line where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, I didn't get an answer to your question about the lines. September 1992, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did those lines change in that period according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Specifically my line did not move.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, please don't mark anything on the map now until we tell you to take a certain pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the map please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, could you use a black marker to indicate first the places where your line was, as you say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, this line -- could you please tell us what the streets that the line passes through -- could you explain to us more specifically which area it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: This area doesn't go through any streets. It goes from Cenex at Stup to River Dobrinja. So this is the Kasindolska Cesta part. It crosses the highway, the main road, through the florists. Then it goes along the edge of the barracks all the way to the top of the barracks, then goes to a part of the Stupsko hill up to the institute for the blind in Nedzarici. Specifically I was -- and I will put a point here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, when you drew this line, you said that it did not pass through any street. Can you please tell us, was it parallel to any street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: With the street Aleja Bosne Srebrene that is the name of the street now, but it was formerly the Branka Bujica street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us that the street Aleja Branka Bujica from September 1992 until 1993 and August 1994 was that street open and could people pass through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: It was on our territory but it was shot at every day from the high-rise buildings around us, so that it was very risky. It was possible only to move through our neighbourhood only at night either on foot or in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you drew this line, could you please tell us according to you how long was the front line that you covered together with your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: We covered approximately 2.000 metres or perhaps a little more of the line. I'm not quite sure how much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the depth of the area of responsibility of your company, so its depth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The area of responsibility in depth was about 200 [as interpreted] metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, in the beginning you said that your line started from Cenex. Could you please indicate the place where the Cenex facility is, and can you please clarify what Cenex is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Cenex are newly built buildings. That's probably why they're not on this map. They are buildings which are currently being used as a wholesale business facility, as shopping outlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, you made three dots. Could you put a circle around those three dots and tell us what they are and also put the number "1" next to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: These are large reinforced concrete buildings which were used as entrenchments by the Muslim army to shoot at our positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, could you indicate on this map the places that you personally know were positions of the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Might I suggest that a finer pen is used. We're using up a lot of the map with thick -- thick lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps he could do that if -- if the next marking comes up. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, can you mark on this map the positions that you personally know were positions acted from by the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Should I circle them?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you know that there were several such places, you can circle and mark it with a "2" and then circle another place and mark it with a "3" and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]
