utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, what did you mark under number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: It's a private house, a new house owned by a Serb, an abandoned house because of the fighting. We called the term Ikic's house, to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about any other places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You circled and placed the number "3" next to this -- on this location. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: It's the refrigeration plant, and we were shot at from there by an anti-aircraft gun several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the number 3 indicates a refrigeration facility and that you were shot at by an anti-aircraft gun from there, could you please tell us which weapons were used from positions 1 and 2. Did they use weapons and which weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Mostly infantry weapons, so artillery, hand-held launchers, Zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, before we go on a break, I have one more question: On this map, could you please indicate any other places that you know about in relation to your front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I could indicate many locations. The whole zone in fact was used as a position, since there are high-rise buildings on the Lukavica Road, also at Dobrinja V. And they had the visual possibility to use heavy weapons against buildings. Occasionally they would move these weapons because of their own safety and they would fire at the whole of the neighbourhood according to its depth and width. It's not a large neighbourhood. It's 2 by 2 kilometres. So everything was in the zone of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, my learned friend says that it wasn't specific in the transcript. Mostly anti-aircraft guns and cannon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Mostly anti-aircraft gun and cannon. I will indicate a few other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you're indicating number 4 and 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The last comment by my learned colleague, "my learned friend says it wasn't specification in the transcript, mostly anti-aircraft guns and cannon." I don't understand where that's supposed to have been. If it can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it it has something to do with the -- perhaps the witness can take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should first clarify whether the witness understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could -- could you please move them on again. Do you speak or understand some English or French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know English a little bit, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps given the time, Mr. President, we could have the break and the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could have the break. One of the missing words in the transcript was the word "heavy," and I don't know whether it was any more -- but that's where I had the feeling that it might fill in. Perhaps the parties could deal with it during the break. Let me just first -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If we do not -- let's not discuss it at this very moment, although the use of the French language could serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness does not understand French at any rate, but word pronounces -- the word that I heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones. If Mr. Piletta-Zanin speaks French, you can hear the English translation, Mr. Ierace, but you could not respond speaking English. Let's first listen to what Mr. Piletta-Zanin tells us in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the missing word is the word that you pronounced. It's the word that I heard in the language of the witness and it is not written in the transcript. But I believe that I heard him, and I think the witness very quickly also mentioned some other weapons. He talked about a weapon -- I'm not going to say which weapon it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is, but we know that there are three different calibres of this weapon and we very often have seen in this case we have seen these weapons and these calibres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is the word "heavy" that does not appear in the transcript. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- according to Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness himself used even more specific, more precise words than just "heavy," "heavy weapons." So you may ponder upon this during the break and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue the examination of the witness, I'd like to inform the parties that the Chamber would like to take a bit more time to think about the position of the summaries. And since it doesn't make play a role immediately in the hour to come, we might do that this afternoon. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, before the break you made three circles and wrote "4," "5," and "6," and number "7." Can you tell us, but please go slow, what is number 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Number 4 is the pensioner's home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Our student hostels.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 7?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Number 7 is the building we call Betonara. And if I may, I'd like to add some other positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, I will ask you a question, if you can tell us. Are you telling us that these are the structures through which the BH Army acted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: These are structures which the BH Army used to fire on my neighbourhood throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which type of weapons did the BH Army use from these positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The BH Army used from those structures infantry weapons for nearby targets and anti-aircraft weapons for more distant areas, and from other positions it used mortars of all calibres, anti-aircraft guns, and from the area of Igman they launched -- well, the term that we use in the colloquial, the cassette bombs, or Savs [phoen]. These are mines for the large-scale destruction of soldiers, of troops of major power.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, before you tell us something about the location and positions of the BH Army, can you tell us -- can you tell us on this map, opposite the place where you made a circle, a black one, can you see the faculty of theology, the school of theology?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, in whose area of responsibility was the school of theology?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP4, in relation to the school of theology and the street Aleja Bosne Srebrene, that is, in relation to your lines, can you tell us where were the front lines of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you then take the thin black marker -- or, that is, you can use a slightly thicker marker because we are talking about lines. If you can, will you use -- make a dotted line to mark the BH Army's positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, is that green?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the witness is now using a green pen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes. It should be blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should even be black, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you remove your elbow so that we can see. Mr. DP4, as said, to make it clear, when the Defence asked you about the school of theology and you said it was in the area of responsibility of the Army of Republika Srpska, can you show where was the separation line in relation to the school of theology.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Facing a particular segment of the front line or all of them? This here is the school of theology.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. DP4. But in relation to the school of theology, when we face the intersection, this yellow line here, can you tell us, this yellow line below the school of theology, what street is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The yellow line -- the yellow line is the street Magistar Niput [phoen] that is the highway -- the motor way Sarajevo -- airport Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the Sarajevo airport, can you mark the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: You mean in the direction of the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you can move the map slightly upwards so that we can see what you are doing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you tell us, what is it that you are drawing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I am drawing the line held by the Army of Republika Srpska in the direction of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you next to it also draw the lines held by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, I made a mistake. You should have drawn it with a dotted line. So could you please just make it bolder with a dotted line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, in relation to the line that you marked and said that they were the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska towards the airport, can you tell us whether in that area there were any positions of the BH Army, and what is this area called above, where it says -- where we have these three yellow squares, above? Could you tell us what part of the city is that? Down towards the airport.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: This is the parking lot of the airport. And the locality across it is called Aerodromsko locality, if that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you make a circle around the locality or Aerodromsko and tell us who controlled it if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: It was controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska, and I'll make circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, you have now circled the line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I made a circle around Aerodromsko locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in relation to this line towards which you say is Aerodromsko locality, did the lines shift there and where was the BH Army's front line in relation to what you say is Aerodromsko locality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I did it. In the beginning of the war, they shifted slightly but later on not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the beginning of the war," what period of time are you talking about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, in relation to your line -- to your area of responsibility, can you tell us what view did you have of the airport, or rather, towards the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Concretely, from our front lines the airport -- one could not see the runway. I remember that. Specifically we could not see the runway from our front lines, not further from the barracks and on. We couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the building of the school of theology, 1992 - and I'm referring to the period from September 1992 to 10th of August, 1994 - do you know who used that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the school of theology was the medical service of the Nedzarici Battalion. It was used -- in front of it there were mortars, and it was used to quarter those people from the military medical service. An APC and two civilian vehicles were at the disposal of the medical military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you tell us - so we are talking about the same period, September 1992, August 1994 - were members of the United Nations of UNPROFOR present in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: UNPROFOR members were present often at certain points in the locality of Nedzarici. For instance, the checkpoint toward -- shall I circle it so that everybody knows?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you have any knowledge of that, then circle it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And put a cross inside the circle and write -- circle with the cross is UN. Thank you, Mr. DP4. Are there any other locations that you know were used by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, the old people's home. And they would be there for several days without leaving it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the old people's home," can you point at it on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are marking, Witness DP4, could you please bend over a little bit less, because we now see the back of your head rather than the markings you make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you mark the place that you say was the old people's home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that UNPROFOR was present there and quite often for a while, can you tell us what period of time are you mentioning when you say "often," and how often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In their capacity of observers and humanitarian activists, they cooperated very well with the personnel of the old people's home. And from the very beginning of the war until the end, they -- Now, how often? Very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "very often," can you say in terms of a week or a month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Several times a week. Sometimes for a whole fortnight without ever leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you tell us, since you marked for us the front lines of the two sides, can you tell us -- according to you, what was the distance in relation to the -- the lines in relation to your front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Depends. Between 20 and 70 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you marked the places, you ended with the positions from which the BH Army acted. And the last number was number 7. And you said that you also were aware of other places from -- which were the positions from which the BH Army operated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you point to them on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The whole row of tall buildings in our area, from Alipasino and Vojnicko Polje to Dobrinja V, and also -- also from the top of Mojmilo, from the area of the reservoir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you circle the area of the reservoir and write inside the circle "RZ," so that we can know that in the circle which says "R" is the reservoir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the circle below the reservoir on Mojmilo were UNPROFOR troops. And below them there were several trenches. And they had mortars, anti-aircraft machine-gun, and a gun -- I am not sure what was its calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, when you marked these places on this map and drew the lines, can you tell us, between 1992 and 1994, in this area which you marked was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Fighting was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, you said that you were issued with a rifle. Can you tell us what weapons did your company have in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The company in my area of responsibility, the infantry company, had infantry weapons. In the beginning they were just ordinary M-48 rifles, semi-automatic rifles and diverse other weaponry. Later on, I was issued with an automatic rifle, and the majority too -- we were -- we kept also some of the semi-automatic weapons and some machine-guns, which were pretty outdated, that is, Brownings from 1937 or something, Sarac and such like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, in your area, how did you communicate with your superior unit? Did you communicate with them? And if yes, then how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In the -- at the outset there was no communication at the very outset. However, after the early attacks, when some kind of a defence line was established, from the barracks which we took over when the Yugoslav army pulled out, we brought induction telephones, which are connected together by a wire and which were used as a basic means of communication with the company in our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who commanded your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Bozidar Cvijetic was the commander in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in the beginning," can you tell us what time you are talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The time until the beginning of 1993 -- or mid-1993. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: It was a young man nicknamed Gasi, and he was followed by Ljubo Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP4, can you tell us whether there were any professionals in your company? By this, I mean trained officers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: There were no trained officers in our company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague will take over to make the whole examination more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. You still have on the ELMO to your right the map which represents that part of Sarajevo. I'd like you to take the pointer to -- pointer, I'm saying. Will you please take up your pointer and show us the area of Nedzarici on the map which is to your right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the witness followed the request and drew roughly the contours of the area around the word "Nedzarici," towards the airport area, and closed the loop by the building called the school of theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in this area, in the area of Nedzarici, were there at the time that we are talking about, was there any destruction? And I'm talking about the destruction of buildings, of structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not clear in my mind which period that is. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are talking about the period that was mentioned a moment ago, that is, September 1992 and 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please -- could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, buildings were destroyed in Nedzarici, and it happened throughout the period of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already asked that another exhibit be prepared. It is D1761, I believe. But as we are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. waiting for it, I'll ask you some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was, witness, the scope of -- the scale of the destruction in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: The scale of destruction was -- well, there was permanent shelling of our area, so that buildings and other structures were gradually damaged; some more, some less. But there was no house which went unscathed, which was not damaged in this -- in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were those military facilities, civilian facilities, civilian residential buildings or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And meanwhile, could we have D1761 prepared for me, Exhibit D1761?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: All types of buildings, regardless of whether they were civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And can you -- how do you explain this destruction, witness, from your point of view, from your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: I suppose they wanted to neutralise a military target or troops deliberately or not. I cannot be the judge of that. Or by mistake they hit both the targets that were aimed or targets that were close by or further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would have thought that when my learned colleague asked that question, he had a particular source of information in mind which was admissible. Apparently from the answer, there is not. It's speculative, and in my respectful submission, the answer should be struck out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will continue along in the same vein. I should like to continue in the same vein, to see whether it is speculation or something else, and I believe that exhibit is D1762 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first -- yes. I imagine that you'd like to continue, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any communication that was -- I just heard something which was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The witness wanted to speak to you. I told him it was not the right time to do so, in order to avoid any interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's up for me to decide whether it's the right time for the witness to speak to me. But let me first give an answer to the objection. The question asked for an explanation. Anyone could explain whatever situation whether it's the right explanation or not. Striking out is not usually the one we use. The Chamber is aware of the objection -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You may recall that exactly the same issue arose with the same witness: Same question, same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And on that occasion, the question was -- well, in essence the indication was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- Of course we have -- I must even admit that the Chamber has asked for explanations of situations that might be in need of some explanation as well, just in order to hear what the witness would tell us. And of course it very much depends on the answer very often whether it will assist the Chamber at all. In general, I would say that asking for explanation of situations that might not be within the limits of the personal knowledge of the witness usually do not greatly assist. I would not say that under no circumstances it could exist, but I think both parties would be wise to refrain as much as possible from -- from speculation on the side of the witness. So if you would keep that in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Also, if you, putting the next questions to the witness, you indicated that -- let me just have a look. Yes. I do understand that with your next questions you'll see whether it's speculation or not. If that does not amount to new speculations, of course you are entitled to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, earlier on you said that according to you it was possible that the damage in all or in part might have been day to a mistake. I'm now going to ask you a number of questions that are closely linked. First of all, you talked about shelling. What weapon was used to shell the position where you were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: Most often mortars, but there was also shelling with cluster bombs from Igman. But most -- for the most part it was the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said that most often they used mine launchers. Do you know if that weapon can -- has a margin of error or not? I'm talking about that specific weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in translation into English we have the term "mine launchers." I'm unclear as to whether that's a mortar or a cluster bomb or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be a translation problem. What word did he use in French? Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I didn't follow your French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution wonders whether there's any translation problem for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, for anyone who speaks French properly there is no doubt about it. A "lance-mines" is exactly the same thing as a mortar. It's exactly the same thing. It's a word that means exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do I need to repeat my question? Were you disturbed by this interruption? Can you answer the question in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP4
utterances.text: In my opinion, mistakes were frequent. Whether while making the calculation or due to some technical problems while shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The objection, I think, should be made in the absence of the witness although at the time. But essentially, if I can -- if you would prefer the witness stays in the Trial Chamber, perhaps I could intimate the basis of my objection. It's a question of whether the groundwork has been laid for this witness to give this opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps better not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I notice -- note one thing: Mr. Ierace raises his objection at the worst possible time. I was asked to be as concrete as -- as practical as possible in order to find out what the witness knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But just a couple of minutes before the break. Perhaps it's best that we ask the witness to leave the courtroom, that he would come back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and that we discuss the procedural issue during the remaining minutes. Mr. DP4, we're not ready yet. In three minutes we will have a break until tomorrow morning. I expect you to come back in the same courtroom at 9.00. And we'll deal with another issue in just a few minutes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. And may I -- may I ask you not to discuss with anyone the content of your testimony in this court. With no one; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you be more specific, as you indicated you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has given evidence that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I gave Mr. Ierace the opportunity to be more specific. But if there's any procedural issue you would like to raise, do you want private session or -- is it anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Not at all. I'd like to remind you that I'm sentenced to total silence when it comes to translation. I need about one minute at the end of the hearing for that. And the time has come for me to submit these mistakes. But I think I should be allowed to do it, because there are important facts I should like to point out. But time is running out for me to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give you one minute as requested. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness has so far given evidence that during the conflict he was armed with an M-48 and later received an automatic rifle. At no stage has he said that he has any experience or training in the use of mortars. I don't know where this line of questioning is going. It ultimately seems to be relevant to whether this witness has a -- an opinion which is based in -- in direct observation -- an opinion on the issue of whether damage caused in Nedzarici by ABiH forces was a mistake. Mr. President, the difference between the -- Your Honours asking the witness a question, as opposed to the Defence asking their witness a question, is that one assumes that the Defence knows what the answer will be. Otherwise, why would they have called the witness? It is not an unreasonable expectation that Mr. Piletta-Zanin has some foreknowledge of what the witness will say and what the basis is. And if it is speculative, then that should be indicated. But this question is without proper foundation. This is a man who shot rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, apart from responding to what Mr. Ierace said, could you also explain to the Chamber what would be the factual basis of the knowledge of this witness on whether hits were -- errors or intended damage done to specific buildings. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly. First of all, I'm only following in the footsteps of the Prosecution. The Prosecution tried to prove that people in Sarajevo -- anyone in Sarajevo was in a position to recognise the sound of heavy artillery weapons, of guns, and was in a position to tell where the fire was coming from. And if anyone on the street is able to gain that sort of knowledge, then that applies even more so to professional military men than to people who were on the spot for three years. In other words, soldiers talk to each other. They acquire additional knowledge about a specific weapon, even if they themselves do not perform these fires. That's the first point. The second point is that this witness, as anyone from Nedzarici, knows the area perfectly well. He's in a position to say: "Here there was a bunker, there a number of private houses were hit. And it is possible to think that it was a fire targeted at our troops and that there was a mistake in the fire. It went too far north, too far south," whatever. Furthermore, the witness will be in a position to tell us about the scope of the damage. And if he tells us, as I think he will do, that the -- all the neighbourhood was the target of massive destruction, there are two possibilities: Either there was a plan to totally destroy Nedzarici -- and I've never heard about it so far -- or there were a number of involuntary mistakes due to the type of weaponry used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the witness make the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the difference between a campaign -- a possible campaign aimed at destroying Nedzarici -- oh, you're talking about that particular point. Well, if, like anyone, he never heard that the -- that international justice tried to find out whether there was a plan to destroy Nedzarici, then he might have come to the conclusion that this damage was due to mistakes because of the layout of the -- of the neighbourhood, very narrow streets, could lead us to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It could not have been else that it would have been errors, because no one ever talked about anything else. And well, my question is: Where here speculation starts and what kind of inferences you are asking from the witness, because your explanation of what you expect from the witness, it seem that is there are at least a lot of inferences rather than observation of facts. I mean, I do understand the first part where you say, "Well, you can ask the witness whether every second or every third or all the houses were damaged and whether it was all done at the same time or that if you have a military barracks, whether all surrounding houses would be hit," but that -- that are all matters of fact. I have some hesitancies as far as speculation comes in, but perhaps the Judges should take the time to consider this and to give you an answer together with the other -- the answer to the other question raised before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to add something. The position of the Prosecution is -- and it's not a secret, because we are trying to find agreements on that -- is that in some neighbourhoods of Sarajevo, damage indicates that there was a campaign. I believe that the Defence is in -- has the right to prove that there were damages in other areas held by Serb forces without any prima facie evidence of campaign. And I believe that the Defence is perfectly entitled to do so. We are not talking here about speculations or presumptions or whatever. If there were -- if these damages happened and if they were done by Muslim forces, then the witness can tell us about them in order to be able to make the necessary comparisons.
